claims.text: Conventional sintering of ZrB2 requires temperatures above 2300 °C.
Spark plasma sintering can consolidate ZrB2 at 1700–1900 °C.
SPS produces dense, fine-grained, low-porosity ZrB2.
The SPS-produced microstructure improves oxidation resistance relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The SPS-produced microstructure improves liquid-metal corrosion resistance relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Rapid, current-assisted SPS enhances ZrB2 densification while minimizing porosity and refining grain boundaries.
Rapid heating and short dwell times promote fast diffusion and particle bonding at lower temperatures.
Rapid heating and short dwell times limit grain growth and processing-defect formation.
Reduced porosity, refined grains, and fewer defects restrict oxygen ingress into ZrB2.
Reduced porosity, refined grains, and fewer defects restrict liquid-metal penetration into ZrB2.
Restricting oxygen ingress enhances oxidation resistance.
Restricting liquid-metal penetration enhances corrosion durability.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have mechanical strength comparable to ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have better oxidation resistance than conventionally sintered specimens processed below 1700 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have better liquid-metal corrosion resistance than conventionally sintered specimens processed below 1700 °C.
The proposed benefits apply when SPS is performed between 1700 and 1900 °C in an inert or vacuum atmosphere.
The proposed service boundary includes cyclic oxidation at temperatures up to 1500 °C and exposure to plating-metal baths.
The magnitude of oxidation and corrosion improvement may depend on SPS parameters and atmospheric control.

contradictions.description: The general hypothesis and falsification rule require superior oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance relative to both high-temperature and lower-temperature controls, whereas the predicted outcome explicitly predicts those improvements only relative to the lower-temperature controls.
